correctness.rationale: The maximal-letter recursive grammar is exact in both directions. Marker-delimited concatenation supplies an unambiguous sublanguage despite ambiguity in the full language, yielding a lower coefficient bound; counting all grammar representations yields an upper bound. The bounds share a unique simple dominant pole because every lower image length exists, establishing exact exponential growth for all alphabets. A forbidden descending pair between two adjacent maximal letters gives an independent strict q-ary image-density bound; binary images are counted exactly. Exact polynomial-convolution identities verify the q=4 sextic. A separately written stack implementation, recursive implementation and full grammar agree on 52389 finite inputs, with the all-length claims proved analytically rather than inferred from testing.

value.rationale: The number of reachable outputs of a fixed-length finite-alphabet stack map is a natural Hartley channel-capacity invariant. A uniform algebraic growth equation avoids the nonunique-concatenation obstruction to exact enumeration and gives a nontrivial strict alphabet monotonicity law. The binary-versus-higher-alphabet exponential sparsity dichotomy is a sharp structural boundary, with a motivated first additional quaternary growth constant. The result covers infinitely many alphabet sizes, not an arbitrary finite numerical extension.
